title: 09-10. Mean, Variance, and Standard Deviation
text:
12 Variance and standard deviation – interpretation
Standard deviation is the typical deviation (either way) from average, not the greatest possible deviation.
Data points often stray further from average.
Variance is hard to interpret – its units are screwy.
Standard deviation is easier to interpret.
We divide by \(n-1\), not by \(n\). Mnemonic: The first data value can’t exhibit variability.
We use \(s^2\) and \(s\) for sample variance and sample standard deviation.
We use \(\sigma^2\) and \(\sigma\) for population variance and population standard deviation.

title: 07. Dataviz: Histogram and Countplot
text:
3 Note on Accessibility:
Data visualization is the production of charts and graphs that reveal trends and interrelationships to the eye. Although it can be done well by and for low-vision and colorblind users, dataviz is fundamentally visual, so it’s problematic for the blind. Data methods by and for the blind should strongly consider other techniques. Nevertheless, it’s important for both blind and sighted students of statistics to understand the larger discipline. I’ve tried to make these notes useful to everyone, understanding that a histogram might not be.

title: 07. Dataviz: Histogram and Countplot
text:
4 Bar Charts (aka Count Plots)
A bar chart represents the distribution of a categorical variable, showing how many data cases are in each category. It answers questions like…

How many of each major do we have on campus?
What home languages are spoken in Potsdam, and how many households speak each language?
How many patients are assigned to each nurse?

To make a bar chart, place the categories (majors, languages, nurses) on one axis (normally “\(x\)”). From each, make a rectangular bar proportional to the number in that category. Leave a gap between the bars. Mark and label the other axis so the counts can be inferred.

title: 07. Dataviz: Histogram and Countplot
text:
7 Histograms – purpose
A histogram is similar, but represents the distribution of a quantitative variable. It answers questions like

What sorts of GPA’s do students on campus have, and which GPA ranges are most common?
How much do Potsdam households spend weekly on groceries? Which amounts are common, which are outliers, and which are unheard of?
Nurses’ visits with patients take a variety of time. How do the durations of visits vary? Are most visits short, or is there a wide variety of times?

title: 07. Dataviz: Histogram and Countplot
text:
8 Histograms – method
To draw a histogram, the x-axis is scaled to show the entire range of data values and divided into equal-sized intervals (e.g. 5-10, 10-15, 15-20) called “bins.” Rectangular bars are drawn above each bin, showing how frequently the data values fall into that range. The y-axis is labeled “count” or “frequency.” Tall bars indicate common data ranges, and short bars indicate rare data ranges. Unlike a bar chart, the bars touch each other.

title: 07. Dataviz: Histogram and Countplot
text:
11 Histograms and Bar Charts – Comparison
In common:

Data values on x-axis.
Frequency counts on y-axis,
Rectangles whose height shows the count.
Applicable to a single variable only (by default).

Differences:

Bar for categorical, histogram for quantitative.
Bar can be freely rearranged, histogram must be in numerical order.
Bar has gaps, histogram none.

title: 04-5. Sampling and Sample Bias
text:
2 Key vocabulary – sampling

Population: All conceivable cases.
Sample: All cases measured and recorded.
Representative Sample: Does a good job reflecting features of the population.
Biased Sample: Skewed, slanted, not representative. Intentionally or accidentally.
Bias: Anything causing a sample to be biased, from cruelty to oversight to unforeseeable effect.

title: 04-5. Sampling and Sample Bias
text:
3 Key vocabulary – bias types

Participation bias or nonresponse bias: You didn’t measure those who didn’t respond, and it might matter!
Pre-screening bias: You must be this tall for the survey.
Survivorship bias: Only “survivors” are included.
Undercoverage bias: Significant subpopulations were missed.
Geographic bias: Selecting from a town, street corner, etc.

title: 04-5. Sampling and Sample Bias
text:
4 A pollster’s dilemma
Which of these should a political polling organization accomplish in order to responsibly estimate the outcome of an upcoming election?

Interview lots and lots of people.
Include a diversity of people (in age, race, hometown, education, etc) roughly in accord with the population.
Predict who probably will not vote in the election.
Prompt the “undecided” to predict their decision.
Draw no inference when people refuse to participate.

(Good political polling is very, very hard!)

10 Key vocabulary – Sampling strategies

Simple (SRS): Select from one flat list.
Stratified: Identify strata of interest, sample some of each stratum.
Cluster: Divide into convenient clusters. Randomly select some clusters. Take all of each selected cluster.
Multistage: Like cluster, but take some of each selected cluster.

2 Vocabulary for relationships

Dependent / Associated / Correlated: Some statistical relationship exists
Positive Correlation: Higher x values linked to higher y values
Negative Correlation: Higher x values linked to lower y values
Independent: The variables are unrelated. No relationship exists.
Explanatory and Response variables: Variables causing an effect, or being effected, or expected to.
Correlation Coefficient \(\rho\): A numerical measurement of correlation. The output of df.corr()

4 Correlation Coefficient
Just how correlated are two numerical variables?
The correlation coefficient \(\rho\) measures strength and direction of correlation.
Use df.corr(numeric_only=True) to calculate.
\(\rho\) nearly 1: x and y are strongly positively correlated.
\(\rho\) nearly 0: x and y are independent, at least not linearly correlated.
\(\rho\) nearly -1: x and y are strongly negatively correlated.
Correlations quickly flag trends and interrelationships for further study.

text:
11 The empirical rule (68-95-99.7)
(Graphic used with permission, Wikimedia Foundation)
Percentiles and tail areas A distribution is N(100,102). How much data should be expected above 120? A distribution is N(60, 22). How much data should be expected below 54? A distribution is N(10, 52). How much data should be expected above 16? Use the empirical rule or choose a cdf calculation tool: Matt Bognar’s CDF calculator Use Jupyter from scipy import stats stats.norm.cdf(2) Use a Z-table (this is the old school method).
Z-score Intro: So, is that a lot then? A certain pet parrot’s body temperature is 107°. What more would you need to know, before judging whether the body temperature is a health concern?
So, is that a lot then? A certain pet parrot’s body temperature is 107°. The average body temperature for the species is 105°. Of course, the parrot is 2° warmer than average. What other general stats about parrots and their temperatures would be useful to contextualize this information?
So, is that a lot then? A certain pet parrot’s body temperature is 107°. The average body temperature for the species is 105°. Of course, the parrot is 2° warmer than average. The standard deviation of body temp is 1.4°. Is the bird’s temperature normal, somewhat high, or very high? Why?
Judging relative to the distribution Judging a data value x relative to the distribution it’s in requires both: Comparison to the mean of the distribution: subtract μ Conversion to units of standard deviations: divide by σ Thus the formula: Z-score = (data value - μ) / σ The Z-score acts like a interchangeable standard of unusualness, scaled to the distribution the data belongs to.
Z-score = (value - μ) / σ It counts the number of standard deviations from the mean, which is a statistically “fair” across different distributions. Z = 0: Average. Z = +1, -1: Uninteresting. Z = +2, -2: Raise eyebrow. Z = +3, -3: Remarkable. Z = +5, -5: Stunning. Interpreting the Z-score
Z score A distribution for test scores is normally distributed N(500, 502). You score 625. Well done! What is your Z score? An LED manufacture process produces units with illumination N(50,0.22). One particular bulb has illumination 49.4. What is its Z-score? If we reject any bulb at 49.4 or below, how much of the inventory would we waste? By reconfiguring the assembly process, we can make the distribution N(51, 12). How would you describe the effect of this change?
The rarity of a Z-score: the p-value A good measure of the unusualness of a Z-score is the portion of the curve at least as extreme as that score. Use Bognar’s tool to answer: How much of the normal distribution is above Z = 2.3? How much of the normal distribution is more extreme, on either side, than Z=3.1? Use stats.norm.cdf to answer: How much of the normal distribution is below Z = -5? How much of the normal distribution is above Z = 2.5?
Methods for finding p-value, recap To find tail areas, you can… Use the Empirical Rule with some geometric reasoning. (Z=1, 2, 3 only) Matt Bognar’s CDF calculator (Z in the range -4..4) Use Jupyter (Any Z will do) from scipy import stats stats.norm.cdf(2) Use a Z-table. (Paper method, limited accuracy and range)
Putting it all together Most people tend to score about 550 on a given exam, with a standard deviation of 60. Your score is 685. Good job! What is your Z-score? What is your percentile? An average business day sees about $1000 in sales, with a standard deviation of about $200. Sales were slow today. Only $450. What is the Z-score? How rare is such a disastrous sales day? A 1000-letter sample of English language should have on average about 80 “a”’s, with a standard deviation of about 9. A randomly chosen Youtube video description has 1000 characters but 120 “a”’s. What is the Z-score of this result? How rare is it? Can you think of alternate explanations?

section: 5 When to add? When to multiply?
text:
5 When to add? When to multiply?
A and B are events. Their probabilities are P(A) and P(B).
P(A)+P(B) calculates P(A or B), provided A and B are disjoint (mutually exclusive).
P(A)*P(B) calculates P(A and B), provided A and B are independent.
1-P(A) calculates P(not A).

title: 14-15. Probability Laws
text:
6 Sum law (basic)
\[P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A)+P(B)\]
…when A and B are disjoint (mutually exclusive), meaning they cannot both happen. If events aren’t disjoint, this rule does not apply.

\[ P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A)*P(B | A)\]

Mean does a poor job describing “typical,” because it pulls hard toward outliers.
Median does a better job describing “typical,” because it mostly ignores outliers.

title: 11. Quantile Statistics
text:
4 What is the median?
The median is the middle value by count. Roughly speaking, half the data values are less than the median and half are greater.
Finding the median:

Sort data numerically
Find the center.
If count is odd, median is the middle one.
If count is even, median is average of middel two.

Example data values: 5, 7, 8, 9, 9, 9, 10, 10, 11, 12
Description: Ten data points are presented in sorted order, starting with 5 and ending with 12. The middle two are accented in bold and are both 9.
The median is 9

title: 11. Quantile Statistics
text:
5 What is the median?
1, 2, 3, 0, 1, 2, 9 ← Median is not zero. Sort first!
0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 9 ← Median is 2.
0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 96 ← Median is still 2.
The median is insensitive to outliers and individual data errors. The mean is not. This is one reason the median is often preferred.

title: 11. Quantile Statistics
section: 7 Median is more informative than Mean
text:
7 Median is more informative than Mean
Most reports on “typical” American finances use quantile statistics – median household income, median net wealth, median rent, median house price, etc.
In highly unequal societies, measures of wealth are strongly skewed right. Usually median is much smaller than mean.
In the U.S., median income is currently about 2/3 of the average income (Source: SSA).
No single statistic describes the distribution fully, but the median often does a better job capturing what’s typical or normal.

title: 11. Quantile Statistics
text:
8 Quartering the data
After sorting a data series, we can make equal quarters by further subdividing each half. Just like cutting an apple:
5, 7, 8, 9, 9 | 9, 10, 10, 11, 12
Description: Ten data points are presented in sorted order, starting with 5 and ending with 12. The middle two are accented in bold and are both 9. The third data point, an 8, central within the left half, is accented. The eighth data point, a 10, central within the right half, is also accented.
From this division we can construct the five-number summary:
Min=5, Q1 = 8, Median = 9, Q3 = 10, Max = 12.
These numbers can also be obtained using .describe():

The five number summary is the foundation of the box plot.

It’s not literally true that a quarter of the data lies between Q1 and Q2. If \(n=10\), how could it be? But such statements are usually nearly true for large and continuous datasets.

2 The Language of Probability
Any process that leads to an unpredictable result is a random process. It can be…

“Truly” randomized: coin flip, card draw, die roll, quantum measurement, etc.
Complex and unpredictable: Weather, voting, disease spread, manufacturing error, a two-year-old’s mood, etc.

A random variable is any variable (numeric or categorical) which depends on a random process.

Result of a coin flip (“H”) or die roll (“3”)
The day’s temperature
Number of students who enroll in a class.
The age, height, or religion of a person (randomly selected from a population).

title: 12-13. Probability and Counting
text:
3 The Language of Probability
The Sample Space is the set of outcomes of a random process.

All possible results of four coin flips.
All possible orderings of a standard deck of 52 cards.
All possible rolls of two dice.
All possible weather patterns today.

An Event is a single outcome or a collection of outcomes.

All four coins land heads (single outcome), or more heads than tails (collection of outcomes)
Cards in sorted order, or top card is 2❤️

Two dice total 12 (one outcome), or total 7 (collection)
Rainy (collection of outcomes)

title: 12-13. Probability and Counting

4 The Language of Probability
For any event \(A\), \(P(A)\) mean its probability.
If we flip a coins, \(P(\) It lands heads \() = 1/2\)
If we roll two dice, \(P(\) Each lands 6 \() = 1/36\)
Often…
\(P(A) = \frac{ \text{Number of successful outcomes} }{\text{Number of outcomes}}\)

title: 12-13. Probability and Counting

A probability is always a number between 0 and 1. For each expression, what probability is meant?

title: 12-13. Probability and Counting
text:
6 Probabilities by counting
\(P(A) = \frac{ \text{Number of successful outcomes} }{\text{Number of outcomes}}\)
I rolled three dice and they totaled 5. What are the chances!

Identify the random process: Roll three dice
Count all possible outcomes, using multiplication.
Count all outcomes which lead to a total of \(5\). Hint: Just list them. 1+2+2 is different from 2+2+1.
Divide for the probability.

title: 12-13. Probability and Counting
text:
7 Equally probable outcomes
\(P(A) = \frac{ \text{Number of successful outcomes} }{\text{Number of outcomes}}\) is only sometimes warranted


Formula works for:

The two results of a coin flip.
The six results of a die roll.
The 36 results of two die rolls.
The 52 results of a card draw from a deck.


Formula fails for:

The 11 resulting totals (2 through 12) from rolling two dice.
The two possible results (positive/negative) from some bloodwork.
The two possible winners of a game.
The six people she might ask for help.

title: 12-13. Probability and Counting
text:
8 Winning a contest.
The problem: Two sports teams (A and B) are about evenly matched: Any game between them is a 50/50 toss up. They play five games. What is the probability that team A wins at least four?
Step 1: What are the “outcomes”?
Step 2: How many outcomes are possible? Multiplication is your friend!
Step 3: How many outcomes are successes?
Divide and conclude.
Bonus: You watch a contest between two teams, and one team wins four games out of five. How confident should you be that the winning team is actually better?

title: 12-13. Probability and Counting
text:
9 A Flawed Classic
The problem: A Dad of exactly two kids is asked whether he has a daughter. “Yes” he replies, but does not elaborate. You take this to mean he has at least one daughter. What is the probability that he also has a son?


Option 1: The other kid
The other kid could be male or female. P(son) = 1/2.

Option 2: Family structures
Four equally likely kid-gender outcomes are possible: MM, MF, FM, FF. Eliminate the first. Of the remaining 3, two are “successes.” P(son) = 2/3.


Which argument is more correct?
This classic puzzle depends on several oversimplifications about the world. Identify them.

title: 12-13. Probability and Counting
text:
10 The Monty Hall Problem
This famous math problem is named after Monty Hall, the host of an old game show called “Let’s Make a Deal.”

You’re in a game show in which you have to make a choice between three doors. One door hides a prize, and two doors hide nothing of value. Whenever this game is played, the host waits for the contestant to choose, then opens and reveals a door which has no prize. Afterwards, the contestant may change their choice before the final reveal. Should you switch to the other door before the big reveal?



It doesn’t matter. A door has been wasted, leaving a 50/50 chance of success with either remaining door.

You should switch. The initial choice has 1/3 chance, and the remaining door a has 2/3 chance.

2 Review – two multiplication rules

2.1 Multiplication rule – simplistic
(works when \(A\) and \(B\) are independent) \[ P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A)*P(B)\]


2.2 Multiplication rule – full
(just works) \[ P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A)*P(B | A)\]
\[P(\text{drawing two aces}) = \frac{4}{52} \cdot \frac{3}{51}\]
\(P(B | A)\) “Probably of B given A” is a conditional probability. It’s the probability of \(B\), adjusted for condition that \(A\) is known.

U = You are using an umbrella.
R = It’s raining.

P(U | R) asks “When it’s raining, how likely are you to use an umbrella?”

Depending on which two we know, we may use them to calculate the third.

title: 03. Correlation is not Causation
text:
4 Lurking (“Confounding”) variables
Any variable, often unmeasured, that drives a correlation between two other variables. When discovered, lurking variables tend to explain away apparent relationships between other variables.

Coffee consumption and lung cancer are positively correlated. (Really!) We should not conclude that coffee causes lung cancer. There may be lurking variables which we have not considered. One of the hallmarks of critical thinking is not jumping to conclusions.

title: 03. Correlation is not Causation
text:
5 So… withhold judgment forever?

Attendance rate is correlated to class grade.
Laws against trans people are associated to violence against trans people.
Within certain banks, loan acceptance is associated to applicant race.
Cigarette smoking is correlated to lung cancer.

The idea of confounding variables can become a hater’s new excuse to dismiss statistical evidence. In cases where common sense understanding, historical understanding, or controlled experimental support a conclusion, we can’t just wave it away!

Data visualization is the production of charts and graphs that reveal trends and interrelationships to the eye. Although it can be done well by and for low-vision and colorblind users, dataviz is fundamentally visual, so it’s problematic for the blind. Data methods by and for the blind should strongly consider other techniques. Nevertheless, it’s important for both blind and sighted students of statistics to understand the larger discipline. 4 The Scatter Plot
A scatterplot is a visualization of two quantitative variables, appropriate when at least two numerical values are recorded about each data case. The \(x\) axis is given the range of values of one variable, and the \(y\) axis the other. Then each data case is represented as one point \((x,y)\) according to its variable’s values. A cloud of points arises and its shape is a clue to any association between the variables.

8 What’s a Box (-and-whisker) Plot?

A visualization of the distribution of one quantitative variable, an alternative to a histogram.
reveals the full range of data values along the \(x\)-axis.
divides the data range into four “equal” parts, called quartiles

the quartiles usually have unequal width, but
each quartile’s size is adjusted to include exactly a quarter of the data points.
the inner two quartiles are drawn as a box, and the outer two are drawn as “whiskers”
The five quartile boundary points are called: Min, 25%, 50%, 75%, and Max.

10 Whisker Technicalities

Customarily, whiskers aren’t allowed to be more 1.5 times as long as boxes. If a boxplot would be drawn with long whiskers, trim them to 1.5 * [box size], and represent data beyond this length as individual dots. Both Python and OpenIntro do this. You need to know this to answer questions like “what’s the maximum data value?” using a boxplot.
